problem: Existing foundation-model VLN systems such as BehAV depend on cloud LLMs/VLMs for instruction decomposition and goal grounding, causing multi-second latency and no offline operation, and they estimate goal distance with heuristic visual reasoning that gives poor metric accuracy. Small edge-deployable language models have not been systematically evaluated for navigation instruction decomposition.
motivation: Outdoor robots for monitoring, inspection or search-and-rescue often lack reliable connectivity yet must follow natural-language, behavior-aware instructions and reach metrically accurate goals. Compact SLMs and lightweight VLMs now make onboard inference plausible, and LiDAR provides metric geometry that the cloud VLM heuristic lacks.
key_idea: Replace every cloud component of BehAV with onboard models (an Ollama-served SLM for decomposition, Florence-2 + Mobile-SAM Search-then-Segment) and fuse the resulting mask with LiDAR for metric goal localization, with a bearing-only fallback when LiDAR returns are insufficient.
insight: A 7B quantized text-only SLM (Qwen2.5-7B) matches the best cloud API on instruction decomposition (Macro-F1 0.775 vs 0.765 for GPT-5.5, overlapping CIs) while GPT-4 (BehAV's original backend) reaches only 0.512, and quality is platform-independent (spread of at most 0.041 across laptop/Orin NX/Thor). Text-only LLMs beat VLM variants on decomposition. The closed-loop comparison suggests the SR gap versus BehAV comes almost entirely from sensor-grounded metric goal estimation (obstacle-avoidance BFA is comparable), and the stop-and-measure latch removes motion-induced error (GDE 0.01 m vs the 0.20 m moving-platform MAE).
method: Offline language decomposition: a quantized SLM served via Ollama (default weights, e.g. qwen2.5:3b/7b) generates five structured fields (landmarks, navigation actions, behavioral actions, behavioral targets, behavioral costs) once per mission, with the same interface as BehAV's GPT-4 module.

Search-then-Segment perception: Florence-2 open-vocabulary detection gives a box for the SLM-extracted goal description, then Mobile-SAM produces a mask only inside that box (replacing FastSAM segment-all + cloud VLM classification); CLIPSeg behavioral cost map retained from BehAV.

LiDAR-visual goal estimation: project LiDAR points into the image, keep those inside the mask, apply an IQR filter (0.5 IQR) on planar distance, require at least 7 points, take the median centroid for range/bearing and latch the world-frame goal from odometry.

Hybrid goal cost with mode switching: in Point-Goal mode (sigma=True) cost is normalized waypoint distance to the goal; otherwise Bearing mode uses heading misalignment (w_alpha=1.5) plus a speed-deficit term (w_v=0.5) toward a pixel-derived bearing, so the robot keeps advancing when LiDAR is sparse.

Stop-and-measure state machine: Idle→Bearing→Measuring→Precise; when a detection with enough LiDAR points occurs, the robot stops, waits for a settle period, re-runs the full pipeline on a fresh image/scan at rest, latches the goal, then disables the VLM; reverts to Bearing on failure.

MPC objective: J = 2.0*goal + 8.0*behavior + w_obs*obstacle with a two-stage NLopt optimizer; the behavioral cost uses exponential decay (lambda=0.3), and obstacle weight is scheduled 3.0*min(1, d_goal/2) with LiDAR returns within 1.2 m of the latched goal excluded.

Benchmarks: 350 human-annotated instructions in 7 categories with 17 local SLMs and 4 cloud APIs across laptop RTX 4070, Jetson Orin NX and Thor; also a 922-image nuImages landmark detection subset and a distance test at 2–20 m.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-7B (quantized INT4, frozen, via Ollama) for decomposition; Florence-2 + Mobile-SAM (frozen) for detection/segmentation; CLIPSeg (frozen) for cost map

numbers_note: No standard VLN benchmarks (R2R etc.) are used; all results are on the paper's own benchmarks (instruction decomposition, nuImages subset, distance test, real-robot closed-loop). Benchmark names are 'other:' entries and splits are nominal.
results: Qwen2.5-7B reaches Macro-F1 0.775, on par with GPT-5.5 (0.765) and far above BehAV's GPT-4 (0.512), at about 9x lower latency offline. LiDAR-VLM fusion cuts distance MAE from 2.05 m to 0.20 m, and Florence-2 reaches F-score 0.974 in 307 ms versus 0.904 in 3198 ms for FastSAM+GPT-4o. The full system succeeds in 31/32 outdoor trials, whereas BehAV succeeds in 25% (Scn.3) and 38% (Scn.4).
limitations: Closed-loop comparison with BehAV is illustrative and not controlled (BehAV planner uses manual goal entry and lacks a LiDAR obstacle term); evaluation is small (8 trials per scenario, four scenarios, one robot).

LiDAR returns are too sparse for small low-reflectance targets (e.g. cone at 10–20 m), forcing bearing-only mode; instruction decomposition remains hard on contextual/adversarial and wet/winter instructions and does not improve with size in the 1–8B range.
Decomposition is scored against author-annotated ground truth with token-level set F1, and the pipeline is not evaluated on standard VLN benchmarks.
